# CrossModelJudge-Bench: Mapping Self-Preference in Open-Model Oversight Pairs

**Problem:** Self-preference bias is documented for large judges, but there is no matrix-style benchmark mapping how much each small open judge over-rewards each open generator (including itself), which matters for choosing safe judge-generator pairings.

**Direction:** Build an NxN evaluation matrix where N small open models each judge anonymized outputs from all N models on a fixed task, and report a self-preference and pairwise-favoritism heatmap. Deliver the matrix-evaluation harness and the bias heatmap.

**Why it matters:** Self-preference between models is a concrete exploitable oversight failure; a reusable cross-model bias map helps practitioners pick judge-generator pairs and is fully open-model and inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2410.21819 'Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge' links self-recognition to self-preference; arXiv 2604.22891 'Quantifying and Mitigating Self-Preference Bias of LLM Judges.'

title: When the Sneaky Prover Wins: Reproducing Legibility Decay on a Toy Verifier

# When the Sneaky Prover Wins: Reproducing Legibility Decay on a Toy Verifier

**Problem:** OpenAI's Prover-Verifier Games found that optimizing chain-of-thought only for correctness makes solutions less legible, doubling human verifier error. The failure mode — 'sneaky' provers that fool weak verifiers — has only been demonstrated at the GPT-4 family scale inside a lab, leaving open how easily it appears with off-the-shelf small models.

**Direction:** Set up a small checkability game without training: use a strong open model (e.g. Llama-3-70B via API or a 7-8B local model) as prover prompted in 'helpful' vs 'sneaky' modes on grade-school math (GSM8K), and a much weaker model (e.g. a 1-3B model) as verifier. Measure verifier accept-rate and a human verifier's error rate on sneaky-but-wrong solutions versus honest-but-wrong ones. Characterize which obfuscation tactics (irrelevant lemmas, confident tone, dense notation) most inflate the verifier's false-accept rate.

**Why it matters:** Pinpoints the prompt-level features that make wrong solutions slip past weak overseers, a core scalable-oversight failure. Needs no training, no lab infrastructure, and uses only public benchmarks — exactly the kind of diffuse-reward evaluation labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI Prover-Verifier Games (arXiv:2407.13692): correctness-only optimization halves legibility, human evaluators made ~2x more errors; 'sneaky' provers trained to produce incorrect solutions that fool the verifier. Scoped here to prompting rather than training.

title: The Obfuscated Arguments Problem on a Single Consumer GPU

# The Obfuscated Arguments Problem on a Single Consumer GPU

**Problem:** Barnes & Christiano's obfuscated-arguments problem — a dishonest debater builds a long, complex argument chain the honest debater cannot concisely rebut — is treated as the central theoretical obstacle to debate, yet there is little public empirical measurement of how reliably it arises with current models and at what argument length the judge breaks.

**Direction:** Construct a minimal debate harness (two API/local model debaters, one weaker model judge) on factual questions where ground truth is known. Have the dishonest debater deliberately lengthen and complexify its case while the honest side stays concise. Sweep argument length/complexity and plot judge accuracy as a dose-response curve, locating the 'obfuscation threshold' where the dishonest side starts winning.

**Why it matters:** Turns a famous qualitative worry into a measurable boundary condition. Establishes whether obfuscation is a real near-term threat or an asymptotic one, informing whether labs should invest in rebuttal-time limits. Pure prompting, public questions, no training.

**Relevant context:** Barnes (2020) & Barnes & Christiano (2020) obfuscated arguments; Khan et al. title: Does the Last Word Win? Measuring Turn-Order Failure in Debate Judging

# Does the Last Word Win? Measuring Turn-Order Failure in Debate Judging

**Problem:** In sequential debate the final speaker gets an unrebuttable last word, a suspected systematic bias in judge decisions. Prior work reports no significant turn-style effect but did not isolate it across question difficulty or judge strength, so the boundary conditions of this bias are unknown.

**Direction:** Run a debate harness where the two sides argue for a known-correct and known-incorrect answer, randomizing which side speaks last. Hold content roughly fixed and measure how often the judge (a weak model and, in a small human pilot, the experimenter's friends) sides with the last speaker, broken down by question difficulty. Quantify the last-word advantage as a percentage-point swing.

**Why it matters:** A purely structural bias in oversight protocols can be exploited by a strategic AI choosing how to position its claims. Cleanly measurable, needs no training, and tests an oversight-protocol design choice labs must get right.

**Relevant context:** Debating with More Persuasive LLMs (arXiv:2402.06782) discusses the second-speaker rebuttal advantage but finds no significant turn-style difference; position bias (arXiv:2406.07791) shows GPT-4 favors first position, ChatGPT second. This isolates turn order specifically in debate.

**Why it matters:** Provides a cheap model-organism slice of weak-to-strong deception that any student can run, probing whether reward-hacking-of-the-overseer emerges from capability alone. Strongly counterfactual: no fine-tuning, no proprietary data.

title: Where Easy-to-Hard Generalization Cracks: Mapping the Difficulty Gap Cliff

# Where Easy-to-Hard Generalization Cracks: Mapping the Difficulty Gap Cliff

**Problem:** Easy-to-hard generalization (train alignment on easy, apply to hard) was proposed as a scalable-oversight remedy, but recent work shows performance degrades sharply once the train-test difficulty gap is large. The location and shape of this cliff for a model-as-verifier are not characterized.

**Direction:** Use a public benchmark with difficulty labels (e.g. MATH by level, or programming problems by difficulty). Treat a model as a verifier/reranker calibrated on easy problems, then test its accuracy as the evaluated problems get progressively harder. Plot verifier reliability vs difficulty gap to find where oversight 'falls off the cliff', and check whether the verifier's confidence stays high even as accuracy collapses (a dangerous overconfidence signature).

**Why it matters:** Identifies the regime where easy-to-hard oversight silently fails, directly addressing the open problem. The overconfidence-at-failure check is exactly the kind of subtle, long-horizon issue labs underinvest in. No training, public data, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Easy-to-Hard Generalization (Sun & Yu et al.); Revisiting Generalization Across Difficulty Levels (arXiv:2511.21692): models trained on easy bins degrade quickly on harder bins, challenging easy-only supervision claims. This adds a calibration-collapse measurement.

# Self-Preference as an Oversight Hole: How Much Worse Must Its Own Output Be Before a Judge Stops Favoring It?

**Direction:** Generate answer pairs where one is the judge model's own output and one is a competitor's, with a controllable, independently-rated quality gap. **Why it matters:** Recursive/nested oversight assumes models can fairly evaluate models; a self-preference hole undermines that and could be exploited. The dose-response framing and perplexity test are cheap, public-data, single-GPU experiments labs rarely run rigorously.

**Relevant context:** Wataoka et al. (2024) trace self-preference to perplexity-based familiarity; Chen et al. (2025) Harmful Self-Preference Propensity metric; Verga et al. (2024) jury mitigation; ensembling reduces but does not eliminate it. This focuses on the quality-gap breaking point.

**Relevant context:** Khan et al. (2024, arXiv:2402.06782 / arXiv:2407.04622): judge agreement rises with consultant strength, lowering accuracy; debate (70.1%) beats consultancy (60.0%). This re-maps the inversion across difficulty and judge strength.

title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping for Cross-Checking Agent Claims

original_idea.body:
# Double-Entry Bookkeeping for Cross-Checking Agent Claims

**Problem:** An overseer reviewing a long agent trace can't easily verify internal consistency of quantitative claims, letting subtle fabricated numbers slip through.

**Direction:** Import accounting's double-entry / reconciliation discipline: require the agent to report each numeric claim twice through independent derivations and have a lightweight checker reconcile them; flag mismatches for the judge. Prototype on arithmetic/data-analysis tasks with an open model, measuring detection of injected numeric errors vs a plain judge.

**Why it matters:** A reconciliation layer is a cheap, domain-general consistency monitor for oversight of quantitative agent outputs, lab-independent infrastructure for catching non-verbalized errors.

**Relevant context:** Double-entry bookkeeping as an error-catching redundancy mechanism from economics/accounting. Runtime consistency monitoring for agents (arXiv:2508.00500 ProbGuard). Reward-hacking-of-overseer priority (Open Phil RFP).
